title: Compound past and participles
objectives: I can use the Portuguese present perfect (ter + participle) to talk about actions repeated or continuing up to now, and I know which other situations need the simple preterite instead.
I can form regular and irregular past participles and choose between long and short forms.
I can use participles as adjectives, make them agree with the noun, and tell them apart from the fixed participle after ter.
I can say that something has just happened with acabar de, and use já, ainda não, nunca and ultimamente naturally.
I can explain why the accents, cedillas, tildes and consonants in this unit's words are written and pronounced as they are.

example.pt: Terminar a faculdade foi a maior conquista da minha vida.
example.en: Finishing college was the greatest achievement of my life.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: qui is said [ki]; the u is silent, as in que and qui. The n after the o only nasalizes it, so con is [kõ]. Usage: used for personal achievements, not only for conquering territory.

example.pt: Trabalhar fora do país tem sido uma experiência incrível.
example.en: Working abroad has been an incredible experience.
example.literal: To-work outside of-the country has been an experience incredible.

vocabulary.note: Accent: ex-pe-ri-ÊN-ci-a. A word that ends in ia counts the i and the a as two syllables, so the stressed syllable is third from the end, and the third from the end always takes an accent. The vowel is closed, so the mark is a circumflex. The x before a consonant is said [s], and c before i is [s]. For a scientific experiment the word is experimento.

Realizar um sonho means to make a dream come true. It does not mean to realize in the sense of becoming aware (that is perceber or se dar conta). Spelling: z is [z], and a word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default, so re-a-li-ZAR needs no accent.

example.pt: Ela realizou o sonho de abrir o próprio restaurante.
example.en: She fulfilled her dream of opening her own restaurant.
example.literal: She made-real the dream of to-open the own restaurant.

vocabulary.en: to manage to, to succeed in

example.pt: Finalmente consegui marcar a consulta.
example.en: I finally managed to book the appointment.
example.literal: Finally I-managed to-mark the appointment.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: in gui the u is silent and the g is hard (the gu rule from the lesson on sounds), so con-se-GUIR. The infinitive follows directly, with no linking word: consegui marcar, I managed to book.

Spelling: ç is [s] before a, and the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone marks the stress: pro-mo-ÇÃO. The plural is promoções. Also means a sale or special offer in a shop.

example.pt: Ela tem trabalhado muito e merece essa promoção.
example.en: She has been working hard and deserves this promotion.
example.literal: She has worked much and deserves this promotion.

example.pt: A formatura da minha irmã foi no sábado.
example.en: My sister's graduation was on Saturday.

vocabulary.note: From formar, to form or shape. The person who graduates is said to form themselves: se formar, as in Marina se formou.

Accent: no-TÍ-ci-a. As in experiência, the ending ia counts as two syllables, so the stress is third from the end and needs an accent; i has only one quality, so the mark is the acute. The c before i is [s]. Unlike English news, notícia is countable: uma notícia, duas notícias.

example.pt: Acabei de ler uma notícia estranha.
example.en: I just read a strange piece of news.
example.literal: I-finished of to-read a news strange.

example.pt: Recentemente, a cidade tem recebido muitos turistas.
example.en: Recently, the city has been receiving many tourists.
example.literal: Recently, the city has received many tourists.

vocabulary.note: An adverb made from recente plus -mente (see the note on -mente adverbs). The stress is on men: re-cen-te-MEN-te, which is the default for a word ending in e, so no accent is written. The c before e is [s].

example.pt: Ultimamente tenho dormido pouco.
example.en: Lately I have been sleeping little.
example.literal: Last-ly I-have slept little.

vocabulary.note: From última (last, feminine) plus -mente. The accent of última disappears because the stress is now on men: ul-ti-ma-MEN-te, the default for a word ending in e. Compare últimos in nos últimos tempos.

example.pt: Nos últimos tempos, os preços têm subido muito.
example.en: In recent times, prices have been rising a lot.
example.literal: In-the last times, the prices have risen much.

vocabulary.note: Nos is em plus os, a contraction. ÚL-ti-mos is stressed third from the end, so it takes an accent; u has only one quality, so the mark is the acute.

example.pt: A mudança de cidade tem sido difícil para todos.
example.en: The move to another city has been hard for everyone.
example.literal: The change of city has been difficult for all.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: ç is [s] before a, and the an is nasal: mu-DAN-ça. Also means a move to a new home, as in a mudança de cidade.
To move house is mudar de casa or mudar para a cidade X; the reflexive se mudar is also very common. The d is plain before a; the ending r gives last-syllable stress: mu-DAR.

example.pt: Meu irmão tem mudado muito ultimamente.
example.en: My brother has been changing a lot lately.
example.literal: My brother has changed much last-ly.

example.pt: Tenho criado o hábito de acordar cedo.
example.en: I have been building the habit of waking up early.
example.literal: I-have created the habit of to-wake-up early.

vocabulary.note: Accent: HÁ-bi-to is stressed third from the end, so it takes an accent, and the open a takes the acute. The h at the start of a word is always silent.

example.pt: Ainda não me acostumei com o frio daqui.
example.en: I still haven't gotten used to the cold here.
example.literal: Still not myself I-accustomed with the cold of-here.

vocabulary.note: Se is the reflexive pronoun oneself (see the lesson on reflexive verbs), an unstressed small word said [si]. The c before o is [k]: a-cos-tu-MAR.

example.pt: Meu inglês tem melhorado bastante.
example.en: My English has been improving a lot.
example.literal: My English has improved enough.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: lh is one consonant [ʎ], like the lli of English million: me-lho-RAR. Built from the comparative melhor (better).

example.pt: O trânsito tem piorado a cada ano.
example.en: The traffic has been getting worse every year.
example.literal: The traffic has worsened at each year.

vocabulary.note: Built from the comparative pior (worse), as melhorar is built from melhor.
Masculine, even though it ends in -a. Likewise o tema, o sistema, o programa. In pr the r follows a consonant in the same syllable, so it is the single tap.

example.pt: O problema é que o aplicativo não abre.
example.en: The problem is that the app won't open.

example.pt: Ainda não encontramos uma solução.
example.en: We still haven't found a solution.
example.literal: Still not we-found a solution.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the same ç and ão as promoção, so so-lu-ÇÃO, plural soluções.

example.pt: O técnico já resolveu o problema.
example.en: The technician has already solved the problem.
example.literal: The technician already solved the problem.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the single s between two vowels is [z], and l closing a syllable is [w], so it is said approximately re-zow-VER. The ending r gives last-syllable stress, so no accent.

example.pt: O esforço dela tem dado resultado.
example.en: Her effort has been paying off.
example.literal: The effort of-her has given result.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: ç is [s] before o. The ending o gives second-to-last stress by default: es-FOR-ço. Dar resultado, literally to give result, means to pay off or to work out.
Followed by de: desistir de um plano. Spelling: the first s is between two vowels, so [z]: de-zis-TIR.

example.pt: Nunca desisti do meu sonho de viajar pelo mundo.
example.en: I never gave up on my dream of traveling the world.
example.literal: Never I-gave-up of-the my dream of to-travel through-the world.

example.pt: Já adiei a reunião duas vezes.
example.en: I have already postponed the meeting twice.
example.literal: Already I-postponed the meeting two times.

vocabulary.note: Related to dia (day): to push something to another day. Spelling: d before i is said like English j, so a-di-AR is a-jee-AR.

example.pt: Ele superou o medo de falar em público.
example.en: He overcame his fear of public speaking.

vocabulary.note: From the prefix super- (over). The r between vowels is a tap, and the ending r gives last-syllable stress: su-pe-RAR.

example.pt: Tenho tido algumas dificuldades com a nova língua.
example.en: I have been having some difficulties with the new language.
example.literal: I-have had some difficulties with the new language.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: di-fi-cul-DA-de. The d before i and the d before the weak final e are both [dʒ], and l closing a syllable is [w].
Followed by an infinitive. In Brazil acabar is normally in the preterite: acabei de chegar. Without de, acabar simply means to end: A festa acabou (the party ended).

example.pt: Acabei de chegar em casa.
example.en: I have just gotten home.
example.literal: I-finished of to-arrive in house.

example.pt: Ainda não li o e-mail.
example.en: I haven't read the e-mail yet.
example.literal: Still not I-read the e-mail.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: a-IN-da. The a and the stressed i are separate syllables (a hiatus), and no accent is written because the n closes the syllable of the i (as in ruim). The stress is second to last, the default for a word ending in a. In não the tilde makes the nasal diphthong ão and also marks its stress. Ainda alone means still: Ainda moro aqui.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents, stress and nasal vowels in the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
This note applies the first lessons to the words that are new here. The method never changes: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default stress from the ending, and if the two disagree, write an accent on the stressed vowel. An acute accent (´) marks an open a, e or o, and a circumflex (^) marks a closed one. The letters i and u have only one quality, so they always take the acute.

The first group is words that end in ia, io, ua or uo: experiência, notícia, horário, sério, prêmio, salários. In these endings the two final vowels count as two syllables, so experiência is ex-pe-ri-ÊN-ci-a, and the stressed syllable is third from the end. No ending predicts stress that far back, so an accent is always required. The vowel of ên is closed, so it is a circumflex; the í of notícia is an i, so it is acute. Compare tia (ti-a), where the stress is on the i itself and nothing is needed.

The second group is words stressed third from the end for any other reason: hábito (HÁ-bi-to), últimos (ÚL-ti-mos), trânsito (TRÂN-si-to), quilômetros (qui-LÔ-me-tros), ônibus. They all need an accent for the same reason, and the vowel decides the mark. The open a of hábito takes the acute, and so does the u of últimos. A stressed a, e or o that a following m or n makes nasal is said closed, so it takes the circumflex and not the acute: trânsito, quilômetros, ônibus, prêmio, experiência. The h of hábito is silent.

Two more marks keep vowels apart. In Luísa the i is stressed and follows the u, so the name is Lu-Í-sa, three syllables; without the accent, ui would glide into one syllable, as in fui. The accent on the i says that the two vowels are separate (the hiatus rule from the accents lesson, also seen in país). And in promoção and solução, the cedilla makes c say [s] before a, the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, and so the tilde alone is enough: pro-mo-ÇÃO. The plural is promoções and soluções.

Adverbs in -mente lose the accent of the adjective they come from. An adverb is a word that says how, when or how often something happens. Portuguese forms many from the feminine form of an adjective plus -mente: última gives ultimamente, rápida gives rapidamente, fácil gives facilmente. The stress now falls on men, which is the default for a word ending in e, so there is nothing to mark. Recentemente works the same way, from recente, which has one form for both genders.

Finally, the pair tem and têm. Both are said [tẽj̃] in Brazil. The singular tem (he has, you have) is unmarked. The plural têm (they have) has a circumflex, and this is a differential accent, a mark whose only job is to keep two written words apart. It does not make the vowel closed. The same pair exists in vem (comes) and vêm (come).

Third from the end, open a, acute. The h is silent.

Third from the end. The m makes the o nasal and closed, so a circumflex.
A stressed i after u stands alone. The accent shows the hiatus.

Ends in e: second to last is the default, so no accent.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: consonants and vowels inside the participles
grammar.explanation:
A regular participle is the stem of the verb plus -ado or -ido: falar gives falado, comer gives comido. Its sounds follow from the rules of the first lessons, and knowing them once saves you from guessing each time.

The final o is said u, so falado ends like fa-LA-du and comido like co-MI-du. The stress is on the a or the i of the ending, which is the second to last syllable, and that is the default for a word ending in o, so a regular participle never needs a written accent. There is one exception. If the stem of the verb ends in a vowel, the i of -ido follows it and stands alone: sair gives sa-Í-do, written saído. The accent marks the hiatus, as in Luísa.

The letters t and d change their sound before the vowel sound [i]: t becomes [tʃ], like the ch of cheese, and d becomes [dʒ], like the j of jeans. What matters is the vowel directly after the consonant, not the vowel before it. In comido the d is followed by o, so it is a plain d: co-MI-du, not co-mi-JOO. In dito the d is followed by i, so it is [dʒ], and the t is followed by o, so it is plain: JEE-too. In tido the t is followed by i, so it is CHEE-doo. Most of the irregular participles contain a t or d, so this difference matters.

The other sounds are the ones from the sounds lesson. The diphthong ei is said like English ay: feito is FAY-too and aceito is a-SAY-too. A single s between two vowels is [z]: aceso (the short participle of acender, to switch on) is a-SE-zu with a closed e (the vowel of say without the glide), and the c before e is [s]. An s or r that closes a syllable (visto, posto, aberto, resolver) is pronounced differently by region, with a hissing s or sh and a tap, strong r or English-style r. In entregue the gu before e keeps the g hard and the u is silent, and the final e is said i: en-TRE-ghi. In ganhado and ganho, nh is one consonant [ɲ], like the ny of canyon. The l that closes a syllable is [w], so difícil is said jee-FEE-siw and resolver is said re-zow-VER. The accent on difícil is explained in the next note: its stress is on the middle of three syllables, while a word ending in l is expected to be stressed on the last.

Nasal vowels also appear: vindo has an i nasalized by the n that closes its syllable, [ˈvĩdu], and in tenho the e before nh is nasal. Remember that the n or m here does not make a consonant sound of its own; it only marks the nasal vowel.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stressed short words, endings in -l, and the letters x and gu
grammar.explanation:
The two notes above covered accents on long words and the sounds inside participles. The dialogues and readings also contain other spelling patterns, and each follows from the same method: find the stressed syllable, read the default stress from the ending, and write an accent only where the two disagree. This note applies the method to the remaining cases.

Stressed one-syllable words that end in a, e or o, with or without s, take an accent: já (already), lá (there), há (has, there is), só (only), nós (we), mês (month), três (three), é (is). A one-syllable word has no other syllable to compare with, so the accent is the convention that separates a stressed word from the small unstressed words such as a, o, e, de, que and nos, which lean on their neighbors. One-syllable words that do not end in a, e or o are left unmarked: sol, mar, luz, sim, bom. The colloquial tá is a short form of está and keeps the accent of the stressed a. The marks on à and às are the crase from the accents lesson, the preposition a fused with the article.

Words stressed on the last syllable that end in a, e, o or em (with or without s) break the default, so they take an accent: está, até (a-TÉ), avó, porém (po-RÉM), também (tam-BÉM), inglês (in-GLÊS), português, você. The vowel quality chooses the mark, as before: open é is acute, closed ê is circumflex, and the ending em takes the acute by convention. The endings ão and ã are different: they are already stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough and nothing else is written: não, então, são, vão, tão, estão, irmão, irmã, manhã, reunião, solução. Compare está, which ends in a, so its stress on the last syllable needs the acute, with estão, which needs only the tilde.

The default for a word ending in l is the last syllable, as in animal, papel and Brasil. A word of this kind that is stressed one syllable earlier breaks the default and needs an accent: fácil (FÁ-cil), difícil (di-FÍ-cil), incrível (in-CRÍ-vel), impossível. Each has the stress in the place that is normal for words ending in a vowel, but the ending l predicts the last syllable, so the spelling must say otherwise. The vowel decides the mark: open a is acute, and i, which has one quality, is acute. The l that ends a syllable is said w, so fácil is FAH-seew and difícil is jee-FEE-seew.

The endings ia, io, ua and uo count as two syllables in the spelling rule, so a word stressed before them is stressed third from the end and always takes an accent: início (i-NÍ-ci-o), horário, próprio, família, várias, língua (LÍN-gua). Língua also shows the other job of gu. Before e or i the u of gu is silent and only keeps the g hard (entregue, conseguir, aluguel). Before a or o the u is a real sound, said w: língua is LEEN-gwa, like água. Before a consonant or at the end of a syllable there is no silent u at all: in segunda and algumas the u is the ordinary vowel.

The letter x has several values, and the lesson on sounds gave a pattern that covers most words. In the prefix ex before a vowel it is [z]: exercícios (e-zer-CÍ-ci-os). Before a consonant it is [s]: experiência, sexta, and the sequence xc of exclusivos (like any s that closes a syllable, it is said sh in some regions, such as Rio). After ei it is [ʃ], like English sh: deixar, deixou. Between two vowels in other words there is no rule and you learn the word: puxa has [ʃ], próximos has [s].

Two more endings are worth noticing. Verb forms such as acabaram and responderam end in am, an unstressed nasal diphthong, with the stress on the syllable before it: a-ca-BA-ram. A final em, as in tem, bem, ontem, viagem, mensagem and coragem, is the nasal glide [ẽj̃], like 'ayn' through the nose. In viagem, mensagem and coragem the stress is on the second to last syllable, which is the default for em, so no accent is written, and the g before e is [ʒ], the s of 'measure'.

grammar.title: The compound past: ter plus a participle, and what it really says
grammar.explanation:
A compound tense is a tense made of two words instead of one. The first is an auxiliary verb, a helper verb (as ir is in the near future), which carries the person and the tense. The second is a verb form that carries the meaning. In the Portuguese compound past the helper is ter in the present (tenho, tem, temos, têm) and the second word is a past participle. A participle is a verb form that is not tied to a person by itself: the English 'studied', 'eaten' and 'been' in 'I have studied', 'I have eaten', 'I have been'. In Portuguese it is built from the stem of the infinitive, so estudar gives estudado and comer gives comido. The formal name of the whole construction is pretérito perfeito composto, the compound perfect past.

The history explains the behavior. Ter means to hold. The construction began as 'I hold the letter written' (tenho a carta escrita), where escrita described the letter and agreed with it in gender and number. Over the centuries the phrase became one verb meaning 'I have written'. The participle stopped agreeing and stayed fixed, and ter stopped meaning hold inside it. So, after ter, the participle never changes for gender or number: only ter changes.

The tense looks like the English present perfect but covers much less. English 'have' plus a participle does three jobs: an experience ('I have been to Rio'), a finished action with a result now ('I have lost my keys'), and a situation that began in the past and continues ('I have lived here for years'). Portuguese divides these up. Experiences and finished actions use the simple preterite, which the earlier lessons taught: Já fui ao Rio, Perdi as chaves. Ter plus a participle does only one job: an action that has been repeating, or a situation that has been continuing, over a stretch of time that reaches the present. Tenho estudado muito means 'I have been studying a lot', not 'I have studied' once. The literal reading, 'I-have studied much', hides this, which is why both readings are shown in this course.

A practical test: if you can add 'lately', 'these days' or 'for a while', or if English would say 'I have been ...ing', use ter plus participle. If the English is one event, names a point in time ('yesterday', 'in 2019'), or means 'ever' or 'never', use the preterite. Compare Tenho treinado na academia (I have been training at the gym, repeatedly, lately) with Treinei na academia ontem (I trained at the gym yesterday). Because the tense needs repetition or duration, it goes naturally with ultimamente, nos últimos tempos, recentemente, desde, todos os dias and expressions such as há semanas.

Only ter changes, so negation and pronouns attach to it: Não tenho dormido bem. In Brazilian speech an object or reflexive pronoun goes between ter and the participle, as it does between estar and the gerund: Tenho me sentido em casa (I-have myself felt at house). In everyday talk, Brazilians often say the same idea with the progressive (Estou estudando muito, for something happening around now) or with vir plus the gerund (Venho estudando, literally 'I-come studying', an effort that has built up to now). Ter plus participle is still fully natural, especially in writing and with ultimamente.

grammar.title: Forming participles: the regular endings, the irregular group and the double forms
grammar.explanation:
The regular rule is the same as for the gerund: take the stem and add an ending. Verbs in -ar take -ado (falar, falado; trabalhar, trabalhado) and verbs in -er and -ir take -ido (comer, comido; partir, partido; ler, lido; sair, saído). English has the same split between a regular ending (-ed, as in 'studied') and a group of irregular forms ('eaten', 'seen', 'written', 'done'). In Portuguese the irregular group is small: about a dozen very frequent verbs, plus the verbs built on them.

Why these verbs? They are the old Latin participles, which ended in -tus (factus, dictus, scriptus, apertus). Most verbs lost them and adopted the regular -ado and -ido, but the most frequent verbs kept the old short form, just as English keeps 'written' and 'done'. That is why nearly all of them end in -to: feito (fazer), dito (dizer), visto (ver), aberto (abrir), coberto (cobrir), escrito (escrever), posto (pôr). The pattern helps you recognize them. Verbs built on these share the irregularity: desfazer gives desfeito, prever gives previsto, descobrir gives descoberto, reescrever gives reescrito, compor gives composto. Ter, ser and ir have the regular participles tido, sido and ido, and vir has vindo, which is spelled exactly like its gerund; the context tells you which it is, since only the participle follows ter: Tenho vindo aqui toda semana.

A second small group has two participles: a long regular form in -ado or -ido, and a short form which is historically a separate adjective. Traditional grammars give the long form to ter and the short form to ser and estar (next note): ter aceitado but ser aceito, ter entregado but ser entregue. In modern Brazilian usage the picture is looser for three very common verbs. Pagar has settled on pago for every use (tenho pago, foi pago), and pagado is rare. With ganhar and gastar both forms are heard after ter (tenho ganhado or tenho ganho, tenho gastado or tenho gasto). Aceitar and entregar follow the traditional split most reliably: tenho aceitado and tenho entregado, but foi aceito and foi entregue, although the short forms after ter are also heard. The long form after ter is always safe, except for pagar, where you use pago.

Ser and ir have the participles sido and ido, so Tem sido difícil means 'It has been hard' (word for word, 'It-has been difficult'), and Ela tem ido à academia means 'She has been going to the gym'. The à is the crase of the preposition a and the article a, as the lesson on contractions explained.

grammar.title: Participles as adjectives: agreement, state and passive
grammar.explanation:
The same word can do two different jobs. After ter, the participle is part of the verb and never changes. But a participle can also work as an adjective, a word that describes a noun, and then it behaves like every adjective in Portuguese: it agrees with the noun in gender and number, as the grammar-map lesson explained. Compare Ela tem aberto as portas (she has been opening the doors: aberto stays fixed although portas is feminine and plural) with As portas estão abertas (the doors are open: abertas agrees). The test is the verb in front. After ter, the participle is fixed. After estar or ser, it agrees.

The two verbs give two different meanings, following the logic of ser and estar from earlier lessons. Estar plus a participle describes the state that results from an action: A loja está fechada (the shop is closed, right now), A conta já está paga (the bill is already paid). Ser plus a participle is the passive voice. Voice tells you whether the subject does the action or receives it. In the active sentence Eles adiaram a reunião the subject does the action. In the passive sentence A reunião foi adiada (the meeting was postponed) the subject receives it, and who did it may be left unsaid. English builds the passive the same way, with 'be' plus a participle, so this transfers easily. The participle agrees with the subject: a reunião foi adiada, os documentos foram enviados, as lojas foram fechadas. A later unit treats the passive in full; here you only need to recognize it.

The agreement table follows the ordinary adjective pattern: -o, -a, -os, -as. The short participles that end in -e, such as entregue, have one form for both genders and add -s for the plural, like any adjective ending in -e. Agreement also reveals who is speaking: a man says Estou cansado, a woman says Estou cansada, a mixed group says Estamos cansados and a group of women says Estamos cansadas. Many common adjectives are participles that became ordinary adjectives: cansado, preocupado, perdido, decidido, casado, sentado, parado.

A participle can also stand alone as a short reaction: Feito! (Done!), Combinado! (Agreed!), Resolvido! (Sorted!), Dito isso... (That said...). With no noun to agree with, the masculine singular is the default form; when a noun is present it agrees as usual: Problema resolvido, Questão resolvida.

grammar.title: Acabar de, já, ainda não and nunca: finished events use the preterite
grammar.explanation:
The compound past covers repetition up to now. The other jobs of the English present perfect go to the simple preterite together with small adverbs that place the event relative to the present moment. An adverb is a word that adds information to a verb, such as when, how or how often. Já (already), ainda não (not yet), nunca (never) and the structure acabar de (to have just) do the work that 'have' does in English.

The verb acabar means to finish. Acabar de plus an infinitive literally says 'to finish of doing': Acabei de chegar is word for word 'I-finished of to-arrive', and English translates that recent completion as 'I have just arrived'. The logic is clear once you read it literally: you finished the act of arriving a moment ago. That is also why acabar is in the preterite, and in Brazil Acabei de chegar is the normal form. The present, acabo de chegar, is possible but much rarer and more formal. The person is carried by acabar (Ela acabou de sair, Eles acabaram de chegar), and the second verb stays in the infinitive after de. Do not confuse it with terminar de, which means to finish doing something on purpose: terminei de ler is 'I finished reading'. Acabar without de simply means to end: A festa acabou.

Já means already: Já comi, word for word 'already I-ate', is 'I have already eaten'. In a question, já means ever or yet: Você já foi ao Rio? is 'Have you ever been to Rio?'. Ainda não, word for word 'still not', is how Portuguese says 'not yet': Ainda não comi, 'I haven't eaten yet'. The idea is that the situation is still one of not having eaten. Ainda without não means still: Ainda moro aqui. Nunca means never: Nunca vi esse filme. Já can also mean right away: Já vou! (I'm coming!).

A frequent error is to copy English and say Já tenho comido for 'I have already eaten'. Ter plus a participle requires repetition or continuation, so that sentence would present the eating as a repeated pattern. One finished event, or your whole life up to now, takes the preterite. Use ter plus a participle when ultimamente, nos últimos tempos, recentemente, desde or a frequency expression is present and the action repeats or continues: Ultimamente não tenho dormido bem.

culture.title: Formaturas, vestibular and talking about progress
culture.text:
Achievements are celebrated loudly in Brazil. A formatura (graduation, from formar, to form) is a major family event, with a ceremony, a party and often a formal ball, and many graduating classes hire a company to organize it for months in advance. Getting into a public university is done through an entrance exam: the vestibular, a competitive exam set by each university, or the Enem, the national secondary-school exam whose score many universities now accept. A student who passes is called aprovado, literally 'approved', and the news is announced to friends and relatives with the same pride as a wedding. They shower the new student with congratulations: Parabéns pela conquista! (word for word 'Congratulations by-the achievement').

In everyday talk, Brazilians often ask how things have been going with phrases like Como você tem andado? (word for word 'How you have walked?') or Tem feito o quê da vida? ('Have done what of-the life?'). The expected answer is a short progress report with the compound past: Tenho trabalhado bastante, Tenho corrido de manhã. Because the tense describes an ongoing stretch of time, it sounds friendly and interested rather than final. For single past events, people simply switch back to the preterite: Comecei um curso novo, Mudei de emprego.

It is also common to encourage someone with Não desista! and to describe difficulties with the word perrengue (a small mess or mishap): Tenho passado por cada perrengue! Being open about both problems and solutions is a normal part of catching up with friends.

exercises.explanation: The prefix ex before a vowel is [z], as in exame. Before a consonant, as in sexta, the x is [s].

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the participle of sair?
exercises.explanation: Sair ends in a vowel before the ending, so the i of -ido stands alone in its syllable: sa-Í-do. The accent shows this hiatus, as in Luísa. The i has one quality, so the mark is the acute.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Tenho corrido todas as manhãs' mean?
choices: I have been running every morning.
exercises.explanation: Word for word it is 'I-have run all the mornings'. Ter plus a participle describes an action repeated up to now.

choices: Lately I have been eating very badly.
Lately I have been sleeping very badly.
Lately I have been working very hard.

exercises.prompt: To say 'I have never been to Manaus', a Brazilian most naturally says:
exercises.explanation: A whole-life experience is a set of finished facts, so it takes the simple preterite. Ter plus a participle would suggest a repeated present habit. Fui here is the preterite of ir.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I have already eaten'?
exercises.explanation: One finished event takes the preterite with já. Ter plus a participle would present the eating as a repeated pattern.

exercises.hint_en: Yesterday I studied a lot. Verb: estudar.
exercises.explanation: Ontem names one finished moment, so the preterite is needed, not ter plus a participle.

exercises.prompt: Ana says 'Ultimamente tenho corrido todas as manhãs' but 'Comecei devagar'. Why two different forms?
choices: Running is a repeated activity that reaches the present, while starting was one finished event
Both forms mean exactly the same thing
exercises.explanation: Ter plus a participle fits repetition or continuation up to now, with ultimamente as a signal. A single finished event takes the preterite.

exercises.prompt: Which is the word-for-word reading of 'Acabei de chegar'?
exercises.explanation: Acabar means to finish and the preterite says the finishing is done. English renders it as 'I have just arrived', but the Portuguese words say 'I finished of arriving'.

exercises.prompt: Which is the word-for-word reading of 'Ainda não li a mensagem'?
exercises.explanation: Ainda means still, so ainda não is literally 'still not'. English expresses the same idea as 'not yet'.
Acabar de is followed by the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'He has just called'?
exercises.explanation: Acabar de plus the infinitive, with acabar in the preterite and the second verb unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Why are feito, dito, escrito, aberto and posto irregular?
choices: They copy the gerund by changing -ndo to -to
They are the old short participles that frequent verbs kept, and nearly all end in -to
They are preterite forms used as participles
exercises.explanation: Most verbs took the regular -ado and -ido, but these frequent verbs kept their old Latin forms, as English keeps 'written' and 'done'.

exercises.prompt_pt: Ela tem ___ a mesma coisa há semanas.
exercises.hint_en: She has been saying the same thing for weeks. Verb: dizer.
exercises.explanation: Dizer has the short irregular participle dito, which never changes after ter. The d before i is said like j in jeans.

exercises.prompt_pt: Eles têm ___ cartas para a família todo mês.
exercises.hint_en: They have been writing letters to the family every month. Verb: escrever.
exercises.explanation: Escrever has the irregular participle escrito.

exercises.prompt_en: She has been working a lot.

exercises.prompt: In 'Tenho vindo aqui toda semana', what is vindo?
choices: The gerund of vir, used after ter
The participle of vir, which is spelled like its gerund
exercises.explanation: Vir has the irregular participle vindo, identical in spelling to its gerund. Only the participle can follow ter.

exercises.audio_pt: Tenho estudado português todos os dias.
exercises.hint_en: I have been studying Portuguese every day.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ela tem aberto as portas' the participle is aberto, not abertas. Why?
choices: Because after ter the participle is part of the verb and never agrees
exercises.explanation: After ter the participle is fixed. Compare As portas estão abertas, where the participle is an adjective and agrees with portas.

exercises.prompt_pt: As lojas ainda estão ___ a essa hora.
exercises.hint_en: The shops are still closed at this hour.
exercises.explanation: After estar the participle is an adjective and agrees with lojas: feminine plural.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence for 'The windows are open.'
exercises.explanation: The participle used as an adjective agrees with janelas: abertas.

exercises.prompt: A conta já está ___.
exercises.explanation: With estar the participle is an adjective and agrees with a conta (feminine): paga.

exercises.prompt_pt: Minha irmã está muito ___ depois da viagem.
exercises.hint_en: My sister is very tired after the trip.
exercises.explanation: Cansado agrees with irmã: cansada.

exercises.hint_en: The meeting was postponed to Friday.
exercises.explanation: Ser plus a participle is the passive, and the participle agrees with the subject a reunião: feminine singular.

exercises.prompt_pt: O pacote já foi ___ ao cliente.
exercises.hint_en: The package has already been delivered to the client.
exercises.explanation: With ser the short form entregue is used. It ends in -e, so it is the same for masculine and feminine.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a resulting state rather than an action done to the subject?
choices: A porta foi fechada pelo porteiro.
exercises.explanation: Estar plus a participle describes the state. Foi fechada is the passive of an event, and fechou is the active verb.

choices: She has been arriving late lately.

exercises.prompt_en: Have you already seen this film?

exercises.audio_pt: Acabei de ler uma notícia estranha.
exercises.hint_en: I have just read a strange piece of news.

I haven't read the message yet.
answers: Eu ainda não li a mensagem.
